front: The unit of design at a door
back: The OPENING = door(s) + frame + hardware set + wall condition + clearances. Not 'the door'. It is the unit that gets numbered, scheduled, specified, priced, ordered, installed, and inspected.

front: Welded frame vs KD frame
back: Welded: mitred and welded as one rigid unit, set before the wall is finished. KD (knock-down): ships flat, snaps onto a finished stud wall. KD is materially weaker and can often be worked loose. Welded at every opening with a security or fire function.

front: Deadlatch — what it does
back: The small plunger beside the main latch. When the door is closed it rides on the STRIKE FACE and blocks the main latch from being pushed back. Defeats the 'slip something past the latch' attack class.

front: Deadlatch — the silent failure
back: If the door is misaligned or the strike is mislocated, the plunger drops into the strike pocket instead of riding on the face. The latch is now defeatable and NOTHING VISIBLE tells you. Check it against the strike in the field.

front: Coordinator — what and where
back: On a pair with an OVERLAPPING astragal, forces the inactive leaf to close first. Without it the leaves close out of order and frequently NEITHER latches.

front: Why the closer is an access control component
back: An electrified lock only secures a door that is fully closed AND latched. A closer backed off because users complained leaves the door resting unlatched all day. The reader, controller, and audit log all work perfectly and the door is open.

front: What governs the delay value of an aluminum storefront entrance
back: The GLAZING, not the lock. Standard tempered glass is a few seconds. If delay is a requirement, the conversation is laminated glazing or security film — architectural and budget — not hardware.

front: Out-swinging exterior door: the one-line spec fix
back: NRP (non-removable pin) hinges or security studs. The barrels are on the unsecured side. Near-zero cost delta, closes an entire attack class, almost nobody catches it in review.

front: The handing convention
back: Stand on the OUTSIDE. Hinge left + swings away = LH. Hinge right + swings away = RH. Hinge left + swings toward you = LHR. Hinge right + swings toward you = RHR.

front: What 'reverse' means in LHR/RHR
back: The door swings TOWARD the person standing outside. That is the entire meaning. Nothing is backwards.

front: The #1 cause of handing errors
back: Not left/right confusion — standing on the WRONG SIDE. Two competent people get opposite answers if they disagree about which side is 'outside'. Always write down the side you stood on.

front: Handing vs swing vs secure side
back: Handing = physical chirality, set by the architecture, unchangeable. Swing = in/out, often a CODE constraint. Secure side = YOUR design decision, and the only one of the three you control.

front: Card reader placement
back: Unsecured (approach) side, on the STRIKE JAMB side. A reader on the hinge side makes every user cross the door swing, every time, forever.

front: REX on the wrong side — the failure
back: A REX motion sensor on the UNSECURED side shunts the door alarm for anyone approaching from outside. The opening becomes uncontrolled and the log records everything as normal. Survives commissioning because nothing looks wrong.

front: Why a handing error can't be fixed like a config error
back: Cylindrical locks are usually field-reversible. Mortise locks, exit devices, electric strikes, and closers are not — the chassis is machined for one hand. A wrong hand is a lead-time hit and a non-returnable special order.

front: The five electrified locking families
back: Electric strike, magnetic lock, electrified lockset, electrified exit device, electric bolt/shear lock.

front: The question that comes before device selection
back: How does a person GET OUT — mechanically, with no power, no network, no controller? Answer that first and the device choice usually collapses to one or two options. Juniors pick the device then figure out egress; seniors reverse it.

front: Electric strike — the advantage and the trap
back: Advantage: mounts in the FRAME, so no power transfer needed. Best retrofit device. Trap: it releases the LATCH. If the existing lock has a deadbolt someone throws, the credential is decorative — and nobody throws it during commissioning.

front: Why the magnetic lock is a different kind of device
back: It is the ONLY family with no mechanical egress. Every other family gives you a lever or a bar — a physical linkage that works with the power dead. A mag's only release is cutting power.

front: What a magnetic lock forces you to add
back: A REX sensor, a manual release device that directly interrupts power independent of the controller, release on power loss, a hardwired fire alarm release, signage, and a recurring test obligation. Five components and a permanent life-safety obligation to replace one lever.

front: The senior position on mag locks
back: Correct at a small number of openings (all-glass entrances, no suitable lock or frame) and wrong at most openings where it appears. If a mag lock is on your drawing, be able to say in one sentence why nothing else works there.

front: Electrified lockset — the underappreciated feature
back: The INTEGRAL request-to-exit lever switch. It cannot be triggered from the wrong side, cannot be triggered by a passing cart, and corresponds exactly to the act of leaving. Far better than a ceiling motion sensor.

front: Panic hardware vs fire exit hardware
back: Fire exit hardware is panic hardware that is fire-labeled: it ALWAYS latches and has NO dogging feature, because a fire door must be self-latching. Specifying dogging on a rated stair door is caught at inspection, after installation.

front: Door position vs latch position
back: DPS says the leaf is in the frame. Latch monitoring says the BOLT is actually thrown into the strike. A door resting closed with the latch riding on a misaligned strike reads CLOSED and SECURE and opens with a light pull.

front: Sizing a power supply: which current governs
back: PEAK, not standby. A supply sized to standby sags exactly when the latch is trying to retract.

front: Sizing a battery: which current governs
back: STANDBY, not peak. The battery question is energy over time; the supply question is instantaneous current. An ELR drawing 3 A for 250 ms contributes nothing to amp-hours and dominates the supply rating. Getting these backwards is the most common sizing error.

front: The most common 'access control software problem'
back: A VOLTAGE problem. Intermittent, temperature-correlated, worse-when-busy, fine-on-the-bench are electrical signatures. Software fails deterministically. If the log shows a valid grant, the failure is downstream of the decision.

front: Does a bigger power supply fix voltage drop
back: No. Drop = I x R, and R belongs to the conductor and its length. Fixes: bigger conductor, shorter run (relocate the supply), or a higher supply voltage if the device tolerates it. 'More amps on the shelf doesn't put volts back on the door.'

front: Fail safe vs fail secure
back: Fail safe = UNLOCKED with no power ('safe' = for people). Fail secure = LOCKED with no power ('secure' = for property). Both describe only the lock's behavior in the absence of power.

front: Why you never say 'fail open' or 'fail closed'
back: Ambiguous. 'Open' could mean the door or the electrical circuit — and an open circuit de-energizes the lock, which for a fail-secure device means LOCKED. Two engineers can use it to mean opposite things in the same meeting.

front: Why fail secure does not trap anyone
back: The inside lever (or push bar) is a MECHANICAL linkage and is never electrified. It works with the power off, the controller dead, and the building on fire. Fail secure stops granting ENTRY; egress was never electrical.

front: The cost of specifying fail safe everywhere 'to be safe'
back: A building that unlocks itself whenever the power drops — including when someone drops it deliberately. You traded a real security property for a life-safety benefit you already had mechanically.

front: When fail safe is genuinely required
back: (1) The device has no mechanical egress (mag lock — physics). (2) Code requires release on power loss or fire alarm for that opening and occupancy. (3) Stairwell re-entry on fire alarm. (4) A specific documented operational requirement.

front: The five failure modes of an opening
back: (1) AC lost, battery holding. (2) Total power loss, battery exhausted. (3) Fire alarm activation. (4) Access control server failure. (5) Network loss to the controller. Modes 4 and 5 are ACS architecture questions, not lock questions.

front: The mode-2 question nobody asks
back: 'What is true after the battery is exhausted?' A building full of mag locks after the battery dies is a building with no locks. Whether that is acceptable is the owner's call — but it has to be an actual call.

front: Why the fire alarm release must be hardwired
back: A normally-closed contact fails to RELEASED — a cut wire looks like an alarm. A software integration fails to LOCKED and fails SILENTLY. It also depends on two servers, a network, and two vendors staying compatible for 20 years, and cannot be meaningfully tested by the people who will own it.

front: Where the fail state must appear
back: In the HARDWARE SET in the specification, and on the security drawings/door schedule. Ordering happens off the submittal, which is built from the spec — not from your drawing. If the spec doesn't say it, the contractor orders the manufacturer's default.

front: The free egress principle
back: A person inside must be able to get out without a key, without special knowledge, without a tool, and in ONE MOTION — always.

front: What 'one motion' protects against
back: Under stress, fine motor sequences fail. In smoke, in the dark, in panic, a two-step operation (retract the deadbolt, then turn the lever) becomes a zero-step failure. The code is not written for the calm, informed adult who read the sign.

front: The three components of a means of egress
back: Exit access (from where you are to the exit), exit (the protected portion — enclosed stair, exterior door), exit discharge (from the exit to the public way).

front: Free egress is ONE-DIRECTIONAL
back: The door must open from the inside. NOTHING requires it to open from the outside. Securing the exterior side is completely unconstrained — and this resolves most 'lock the exit' client requests, because what they actually fear is people coming IN.

front: Delayed egress — the shape of it
back: Push the bar, local alarm sounds immediately, irreversible timer runs, door unlocks and stays unlocked until manual reset. Releases on fire alarm, sprinkler flow, and power loss. Occupancy-limited, sprinkler-conditioned, signage required, recurring testing required. [CODE][VERIFY every parameter]

front: Delayed egress — the client misunderstanding
back: Clients hear 'delayed egress' and think 'locked'. It is a short, loudly-announced, code-conditioned, self-defeating-on-alarm arrangement with an ongoing testing obligation. Correct it in the first meeting.

front: Sensor-release arrangement — the components
back: Sensor on the egress side + manual release device that directly interrupts power independent of the controller + release on power loss + hardwired fire alarm release + signage. All of it exists to replace the mechanical linkage a lever would have given you free. [CODE][VERIFY]

front: The 'lock the exit' conversation, in order
back: (1) Name the actual risk. (2) State the constraint plainly, once. (3) Offer the alternatives you already prepared — alarm it, secure the outside, delayed egress if permitted, or MOVE THE ASSET. (4) Write it down.

front: Which egress test fails in service
back: SENSOR COVERAGE. A sensor aimed for an adult walking briskly at chest height misses a person in a wheelchair, a person crawling under smoke, and an oblique approach. Test from the awkward directions and at slow speeds — that is who the arrangement exists to protect.

front: Which locking devices need a power transfer
back: Anything electrified that lives IN THE LEAF: electrified locksets, electrified exit devices, electrified trim. Electric strikes and magnetic locks mount in or on the FRAME and need no transfer.

front: The four power transfer methods
back: Electrified transfer hinge (concealed, ~24 AWG, 4/8/10 conductor), electric power transfer / EPT (mortised, higher count, heavier gauge), surface door loop (retrofit only, ugly, exposed), continuous hinge with raceway (high-cycle doors).

front: Conductor budget for a fully monitored electrified mortise lockset
back: Lock power 2 + latch monitoring 2 + REX lever switch 2 + deadbolt monitoring 2 = 8, plus a MINIMUM of 2 spares = specify 10-conductor.

front: Why you always specify spare conductors
back: Cost delta is small and one-time; the cost of needing another conductor after installation is a door removal, and on a rated opening a voided label. Spares get consumed by installation damage (most common), a lock function change at submittal, or flex fatigue in year seven.

front: The transfer calculation everyone skips
back: The circuit does not stop at the frame. Six feet of 24 AWG at 2.8 A drops more than a volt — enough to move the required home run conductor by a full size. Negligible for a 0.3 A lockset; DECISIVE for an ELR device. This is why an ELR gets an EPT and not a hinge.

front: The dominant failure mode of a power transfer
back: FLEX FATIGUE. A conductor that bends every cycle work-hardens and fractures inside the insulation where nothing is visible. Design against it: stranded conductors only, a product rated for the cycle count, and spares.

front: Why door prep is a submittal decision, not a field decision
back: Doors are machined at the FACTORY per the approved submittal. Field-modifying a rated door voids its label. The transfer decision must be fixed before the door order — which is earlier than the security design feels finished.

front: The most common omission in a security drawing set
back: A missing POWER TRANSFER. It happens because the transfer is invisible in every review view: the reader is on the plan, the lock is in the hardware set, the panel is on the riser, and the transfer belongs to none of them. Review for it as a deliberate pass.

front: What a surface door loop on a finished building tells you
back: A design omission that was patched in the field. On a rated opening, probably also a voided label.

front: Why a fire door rating belongs to the ASSEMBLY
back: Leaf, frame, hinges, closer, latching hardware, glazing, gasketing, and anchoring were tested TOGETHER. Substituting a 'compatible' component takes the assembly outside what was tested — and outside what was tested is not rated. Nothing tells you; the label still says 90 minutes.

front: Where fire labels are and what voids one
back: Leaf: hinge edge near the top. Frame: hinge jamb rabbet. Voided by: a hole not in the listed prep, field cutting/trimming/welding, an unlisted substituted component, removing a required component, or painting the label so it can't be read.

front: The four behaviors of a rated opening
back: (1) Closed. (2) Self-closing. (3) Self-latching (positive latching). (4) Unmodified.

front: Why a fire door must POSITIVELY latch
back: Pressure differential across the barrier during a fire will push an unlatched leaf open. A closed but unlatched door is not a barrier. Everything else — no mag locks, no dogging, fail secure only, stair re-entry releasing the trim — follows from this one requirement.

front: Why a magnetic lock is unacceptable at a rated opening
back: Two independent reasons. (1) It holds by magnetic force against a face, not by a bolt in a strike — it is not positive latching. (2) It releases on fire alarm by design, exactly when the door must stay shut. [CODE][VERIFY]

front: Where a card reader goes at a rated opening
back: On the WALL beside the opening — never through-bolted to the frame. A through-bolt is a hole that was not in the listed preparation. Nothing about a reader's function requires it to be on the frame; that is a habit from drawing plans.

front: The only permitted way to hold a fire door open
back: A LISTED hold-open — magnetic hold-open or closer-holder-release — that drops the door on fire alarm. A wedge, a hook, or a fire extinguisher is a violation, and it is always a workflow problem, so fix the workflow too. [CODE][VERIFY]

front: Why 'it closes when I let go from wide open' is an inadequate test
back: The failure is at small angles. Test by releasing the door from about 5 degrees open and confirming it closes AND POSITIVELY LATCHES. That is the test that fails.

front: The obligation your rated openings create
back: Periodic inspection and testing of fire door assemblies (commonly annual, per NFPA 80). It transfers to the OWNER at substantial completion and recurs for the life of the building. Your security components are on the test list. Nobody has usually been told they own it. [VERIFY]

front: Why the mechanical key is the real perimeter
back: Every electrified lock has a mechanical key override by design, because 'what happens when the battery is dead' needs an answer. A person with the right key bypasses every credential rule, alarm, and audit trail — and a mechanical key operation generates NO EVENT at most openings.

front: Change key / master key / grand master
back: CK opens one lock or a small group. MK opens a defined group that each also have their own CK. GMK opens multiple MK groups. Each level up is a skeleton key for everything beneath it.

front: Three costs of adding a level to a key hierarchy
back: (1) Differs are finite and masterkeying consumes them fast. (2) A cylinder accepting more keys has more shear points, so it is mechanically weaker. (3) The blast radius of a lost key equals the level it sits at.

front: The rule for hierarchy depth
back: Mirror the responsibility structure and go NO DEEPER. Most hierarchies are deeper than the organization that uses them, because they were designed once around an org chart that has since changed twice.

front: The control key (SFIC) — why it is the most sensitive credential
back: It removes and replaces CORES without disassembling the lock. It opens no door on its own, which is exactly why it gets treated casually. Lost control key = rekey EVERY CORE IN THE SYSTEM.

front: What a restricted or patented keyway actually buys you
back: The ability to KNOW HOW MANY KEYS EXIST. Blanks are not commercially available and duplication runs through an authorized dealer against a recorded list. Without it that number is unknowable and every other control is built on sand. ('DO NOT DUPLICATE' is a request, not a control.)

front: Why SFIC (interchangeable cores) matter operationally
back: Rekeying is a core swap with a control key — minutes, no disassembly, no locksmith with a lock in pieces. It makes rekeying cheap enough that it actually happens when it should, instead of being deferred until nobody can account for the keys.

front: Construction keying — the step that gets skipped
back: Temporary construction keys/cores give the contractor access during construction and are supposed to be voided or replaced at turnover. Nobody performs the turnover, or does 80% of openings. Every trade that worked on the building retains access, indefinitely, with no record. Assume it happened.

front: How to verify construction key turnover
back: PER OPENING, not in aggregate. For each: install the permanent core, attempt the construction key (must fail), operate the permanent key (must work). Plus a physical count of construction cores and keys, and an owner-selected 10% spot-check. Aggregate certification is the artifact produced when nobody walked the building.

front: When to specify an opening with NO mechanical override
back: At the highest consequence tier only (vault, secure media, cage), where the permanent bypass of every electronic control outweighs the operational benefit. Requires: a written emergency access procedure, a stated time-to-access, and the owner's WRITTEN acceptance. Fire service access is separate and not yours to trade away.

front: The mechanical attack classes and their countermeasures
back: Duplication -> restricted keyway (a POLICY control). Picking/bumping/drilling -> a rated high-security cylinder (UL 437, A156.30). Wrenching -> protective collar. Latch slipping -> a properly seated deadlatch. Frame attack -> reinforcement and anchorage. Hinge pins -> NRP or security studs.

front: The highest-value recommendation you can make to a client with a new access control system
back: Key control — a written policy, one named owner, an issuance register, key return in the HR offboarding checklist, an annual physical audit, and a restricted keyway. It is a policy project, not a procurement, and it reduces your own future scope. Say it anyway.

front: The pattern across lessons 04, 05, and 07
back: Your design creates ONGOING OBLIGATIONS that transfer to the owner at substantial completion and are invisible unless you write them down: delayed egress testing, sensor-release testing, fire door inspection, battery replacement, key control. Hand over the obligations with the system.
